methodological_rigor.justification: The study examines FH535 effects on Wnt/β-catenin signaling and MCP1/MCP2 chemokine expression in two CRC cell lines (HCT116, HT29) using MTT, flow cytometry, Western blotting, wound healing, Boyden chamber, siRNA, ELISA, and RT-qPCR—a standard in vitro methodology panel. All experiments have n=3 biological replicates with appropriate statistical testing (t-tests, ANOVA). The siRNA knockdown validates pharmacological inhibitor specificity. However, major limitations include: only two cell lines from the same laboratory source (no primary cultures, patient-derived organoids, or in vivo validation); single 24-hour time point for most assays without kinetic analyses or EC50 characterization beyond viability; FH535 dual PPAR/β-catenin mechanism complicating pathway-specific attribution; and in silico TCGA/COAD data showing inverse CTNNB1-MCP expression in tumors (contradicting the in vitro direction of effect), which is discussed but not reconciled.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a preclinical in vitro study (Oxford LoE 5) with in silico TCGA supplementary analysis. There is no in vivo validation, no patient-derived material, and no translational bridge to clinical CRC management. FH535 is not currently in clinical development. The MCP1/MCP2 immunomodulatory findings are hypothesis-generating; the TCGA data showing opposite expression patterns between CTNNB1 and MCPs in clinical tumors versus what is observed in cell lines (MCPs decrease with FH535/β-catenin inhibition in vitro but are lower in tumors overall) suggests that the clinical relevance of the cell-line findings is uncertain. The immunomodulatory conclusions require in vivo co-culture, xenograft, or clinical validation before any clinical application.

reporting_quality.justification: Methods are detailed with reagent catalogue numbers, antibody clone information, instrument models, and software versions provided. At least three biological replicates per experiment are reported with mean ± SD/SEM. Effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals are noted as reported where applicable. Limitations of FH535 dual PPAR/β-catenin activity and the lack of kinetic data are explicitly acknowledged. The contradiction between in vitro and in silico MCP expression data is noted in the discussion. ARRIVE guidelines for preclinical research are partially applicable; no animal experiments were conducted. Primary data are not deposited; cell lines are from a named institutional source.

novelty_literature.justification: The anti-proliferative effects of FH535 on CRC cells are well-established (cited prior work in DLD-1, SW620, SW480). The novel contribution is the identification of MCP1/CCL2 and MCP2/CCL8 suppression as downstream consequences of β-catenin inhibition in CRC cells—not previously reported. The THP-1 monocyte polarization experiment suggesting M1-like shift in conditioned media from FH535-treated cells is a modest functional extension. The in silico TCF4-MCP1 co-expression analysis provides a mechanistic hypothesis linking the canonical Wnt transcription factor to chemokine regulation. The immunomodulatory framing adds a new dimension to FH535 pharmacology beyond direct anti-tumor effects.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well-organized and the results sections are clearly written with logical flow from viability to apoptosis to migration/invasion to pathway confirmation and immunomodulation. The discussion appropriately distinguishes pharmacological (FH535) from genetic (siRNA) evidence. However, several passages overstate clinical translatability of in vitro findings without sufficient qualification, and the conclusion section frames FH535 as a 'promising therapeutic agent' without acknowledging that no clinical development program exists. The in silico finding of inverse CTNNB1-MCP expression in patient tumors (opposite to the in vitro effect direction) is noted but inadequately reconciled, representing a meaningful internal inconsistency.

key_strengths: First identification of MCP1/CCL2 and MCP2/CCL8 suppression as downstream effectors of β-catenin inhibition in CRC—a novel immunomodulatory dimension
siRNA knockdown validation provides genetic confirmation of pharmacological FH535 effects, strengthening pathway attribution
THP-1 monocyte polarization experiment provides preliminary evidence for immunomodulatory impact on the tumor microenvironment
In silico TCGA analysis contextualizes in vitro findings within clinical COAD gene expression data, including TCF4-MCP1 co-expression and survival correlations
key_concerns: Only two cell lines from a single institution without patient-derived or in vivo validation; findings may not generalize to CRC molecular subtypes not represented by HCT116/HT29

The in silico data showing that CTNNB1 and MCP1/MCP2 are inversely expressed in clinical COAD tumors (MCPs lower in tumors) directly contradicts the in vitro model in which β-catenin drives MCP expression—this inconsistency is not adequately reconciled
FH535 dual PPAR/β-catenin mechanism precludes clean Wnt-pathway attribution for chemokine effects; siRNA provides supporting but not complete evidence of β-catenin specificity
Single 24-hour time point for most functional assays and absence of in vivo xenograft or organoid validation severely limit translational interpretation
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competent preclinical in vitro mechanistic study identifying MCP1/MCP2 suppression as a novel downstream effect of β-catenin inhibition in CRC cells; the main conceptual limitation is the contradictory in silico TCGA data and the absence of in vivo validation, which together position this as a hypothesis-generating tier 4 study requiring minor revisions primarily to reframe clinical claims appropriately and reconcile the in vitro-in silico discrepancy.
